item.title: Local AI Session Manager Runs in a Single 138 MB Rust Binary
item.description:
Local AI Session Manager Runs in a Single 138 MB Rust Binary

A new self‑reflective AI session manager can run entirely locally from one Rust binary of about 138 MB, embedding SQLite and a vector index, and requiring no containers, database servers, Python, or API keys.

🔍 Overview

  • Single executable (~138 MB) written in Rust
  • Embedded SQLite stores chunks, embeddings, and enrichment state
  • In‑memory HNSW vector index for fast local search
  • FastEmbed provides 384‑dimensional local embeddings
  • No external dependencies such as Docker, database servers, or API keys

🧩 How it Works

  • Sessions start with a concise recap paragraph that states intent, completed work, settled items, open items, and the next step.
  • Every clause in a session can carry a receipt linking to a commit, task, verdict, or correction; clauses without evidence are omitted.
  • Dreams: the system checks past conclusions against git history and marks stale anchors with the commit that changed them.
  • Compaction: after a compact, the system stores pointers to the original turns and can retrieve them via csr_transcript.
  • A companion pane shows what the AI was told, what it missed, and any user corrections.
  • The plumbing layer uses SQLite and a local vector index to search past sessions; the AI can invoke this directly through MCP tools.

⚙️ Key Details

  • CI on 2026‑11‑18: cargo test --locked --no-fail-fast → 6,939 passed, 0 failed, 34 ignored
  • cargo fmt, clippy -D warnings, and actionlint report no issues
  • Installer tests pass 58 of 58
  • Repo can be scanned manually with csr-engine codemap scan --repo <path>
  • Local vector search and embedding generation require zero external services

🚀 Availability

  • The binary runs locally in a single process; no Docker, no remote services, and no API keys are needed.
  • Users can map a repository to enable code‑aware answers across all worktrees.
  • The system integrates with Claude via the Self‑Reflect plugin to maintain session continuity.

#AI #Rust #LocalLLM #SelfReflect #DeveloperTools

Source: ramakay/claude-self-reflect

item.title: RTK CLI Proxy Compresses Developer Command Outputs to Reduce AI Token Costs by 60-90%
item.description:
RTK CLI Proxy Compresses Developer Command Outputs to Reduce AI Token Costs by 60-90%

RTK is a new CLI proxy designed as a cost reduction engine for AI coding agents, reducing LLM token consumption by 60% to 90% on common development commands. Built as a single Rust binary with zero dependencies, the tool operates under 25 milliseconds per command across over 100 commands without changing how you work.

🔍 Overview

RTK acts as a command-line intermediary that compresses test runs, diffs, logs, and builds before they are read by an AI agent. For instance, when an agent runs git status, RTK runs rtk git status and delivers a 3-line summary instead of 40 lines. This allows developers to clean API traffic and reduce token volume without breaking prompt caching. The tool has already seen adoption by developers at Microsoft, Google, Amazon, Meta, Apple, NVIDIA, IBM, Tencent, ByteDance, Alibaba, Shopify, Datadog, SAP, Adobe, Intel, Samsung, Bosch, Cisco, JPMorgan Chase, Oracle, Netflix, Toyota, Salesforce, Siemens, Accenture, Uber, Spotify, and over 1,100 other companies.

🧩 How it works

RTK handles command compression and optimization through several primary mechanisms:

  • Output Compression: Trims and compresses terminal outputs by up to 90% to prevent agents from processing redundant logs.
  • Heavy Read Delegation: Allows developers to hand off heavy reads to a cheaper model.
  • Agent-Agnostic Pipelines: Uses a single configuration file that allows developers to use built-in pipelines, install shared pipelines, or write and share custom pipelines. The top community pipeline reduces total cost by 20.2% in benchmark runs.
  • RTK Pro: Serves as a control layer for AI agents, functioning as a single gateway for AI calls, costs, secrets, personal data, policies, team catalogs, and audit logs.

⚙️ Tracking savings

Every command managed by RTK is counted locally on your machine. You can view your saved tokens and performance metrics using the following tracking commands:

Command Action
rtk gain Displays summary statistics of saved tokens
rtk gain --graph Displays an ASCII graph of savings over the last 30 days
rtk gain --history Displays your recent command history
rtk gain --daily Displays a day-by-day breakdown of savings
rtk gain --all --format json Exports your savings data in JSON format for dashboards

🚀 Availability

RTK can be installed on your machine using one of the following methods:

  • Homebrew (macOS): 
    1

    brew install rtk
  • Winget (Windows): 
    1

    winget install rtk-ai.rtk
  • Shell Script: 
    1

    curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rtk-ai/rtk/refs/heads/master/install.sh | sh

To initialize the proxy for Claude Code and other agents, run the hook registration command:

1

rtk init -g

#rtk #AIagents #LLM #DeveloperTools #Rust

Source: rtk-ai/rtk

item.title: NVIDIA Frontend‑Crates Enable Robust Tool‑Call Parsing for LLM Agents
item.description:
NVIDIA Frontend‑Crates Enable Robust Tool‑Call Parsing for LLM Agents

A new parser built with NVIDIA’s frontend‑crates demonstrates how to reliably extract tool calls, reasoning, and visible text from streamed LLM output.

🔍 Overview

  • Tool calls can arrive in pieces, arguments can be cut short, and model‑specific markup can leak into the answer.
  • The frontend parser converts raw output (token IDs or decoded text) into three streams: visible text, reasoning, and tool calls.
  • A protocol adapter then translates these events into an OpenAI‑compatible response for both batch JSON and streaming updates.

🧩 How It Works

  1. Prompt preparation – The frontend tokenizes the prompt and sends it to the inference engine, which generates tokens.
  2. Parsing – The parser consumes token IDs or decoded text, separating reasoning, visible text, and tool calls in order.
  3. Emission Rules – The parser decides when to emit data, when to buffer, and how to handle the end of the stream to avoid premature syntax leaks or delayed ordinary text.
  4. Recovery – With malformed or incomplete calls, the parser follows documented recovery rules instead of guessing the model’s intent.
  5. Validation – If the model names an unavailable tool, the parser reports the call; a serving layer validates tool availability, authorization, schema, and policy.

⚙️ Key Challenges

  • Boundary handling – Calls may be split across chunks; markers can appear inside arguments; ordinary text can surround calls.
  • Incomplete data – The model might stop halfway through a city name or omit a required tool name, requiring the parser to buffer until the call is complete.
  • Leak prevention – Emitting too early leaks markup into the answer; waiting too long delays normal text.
  • Wrong tool selection – Even a syntactically valid call can be the wrong choice for the user’s request.

🧪 Testing & Conformance

  • Conformance Corpus – Frontend‑crates pair model outputs with expected results using language‑neutral YAML fixtures, allowing Rust parsers and Python references to run identical cases.
  • Regression tests – Cover leaked markup, duplicate calls, lost arguments, and can be adapted to other model families.
  • UNIFIED. cases* – For a new parser, start with all UNIFIED.* cases across model families; they include complete, malformed, truncated, multiple, interleaved calls, streaming boundaries, and end‑of‑input behavior.

🚀 Practical Example

  • The tutorial starts with a weather request (get_weather with a city argument) and a human‑reviewed test set.
  • Using frontend‑crates, the parser correctly extracts the reasoning, the visible response, and the get_weather call even when the city name is split across streaming chunks.

💡 Why It Matters

  • Consistent grammar and recovery policy let the parser preserve valid data without inventing calls or leaking model‑specific markup.
  • Accurate parsing enables downstream services to validate tool availability, enforce policies, and provide reliable AI‑agent behavior.

#ToolCalling #LLMParsing #Rust

Source: Build Tool-Calling Parsers in Rust with AI Agents | NVIDIA Technical Blog

item.title: GeoLibre Releases Pure-Rust Geospatial Toolkit Compiled to WebAssembly
item.description:
GeoLibre Releases Pure-Rust Geospatial Toolkit Compiled to WebAssembly

GeoLibre has released a new pure-Rust geospatial toolkit compiled to WebAssembly, enabling client-side geospatial processing without requiring servers, native installations, or GDAL dependencies. The toolkit is available as an npm package (geolibre-wasm) and PyPI package (geolibre-wasm) and ships with both the existing whitebox-wasm tools and new GeoLibre-authored tools located in the geolibre-tools crate. The release includes a self-contained demo page that loads all tool manifests and allows users to run geoprocessing on sample or custom GeoTIFF files entirely in the browser, with support for viewing exit codes, stdout, output files, and download links.

#GeoLibre #WebAssembly #Geospatial #Rust #GIS #SpatialAnalysis

item.title: AI Agents Rewrite Curl in Rust While Original Project Adds 400 Bugfixes
item.description:
AI Agents Rewrite Curl in Rust While Original Project Adds 400 Bugfixes

🔍 Overview

During a period when AI agents converted 185,000 lines of C code into 340,000 lines of Rust code, the actual curl project merged over 300 commits.

⚙️ Key details

The original curl project improved during this timeframe of a little more than three weeks, incorporating:

  • Over 200 bugfixes that the Rust rewrites did not include.
  • Fixes for a few vulnerabilities.
  • An additional 200 bugfixes in the following month, along with maybe a few more vulnerability fixes.

💡 Why it matters

The evidence highlights a comparison between the static output of the AI rewrite and the ongoing maintenance of the source project. The text asks whether these clones will keep up with the actual development pace of the original software.

#curl #Rust #AIagents #SoftwareRewrite #Bugfixes

Source: A quote from Daniel Stenberg

item.title: FastEmbed: Rust Library for Local Vector Embeddings
item.description:
FastEmbed: Rust Library for Local Vector Embeddings

FastEmbed is a Rust library for generating vector embeddings and reranking locally. It supports synchronous usage without requiring a Tokio runtime and uses ONNX inference and fast encodings for performance.

🔍 Overview

  • FastEmbed is a Rust library for generating vector embeddings and reranking locally.
  • It supports synchronous usage without requiring a Tokio runtime.
  • Uses ONNX inference and fast encodings for performance.

⚙️ Key Details

  • Uses @pykeio/ort for performant ONNX inference.
  • Uses @huggingface/tokenizers for fast encodings.

🚀 Availability

  • Python: fastembed
  • Go: fastembed-go
  • JavaScript: fastembed-js

💡 Why it matters

  • FastEmbed provides a local solution for generating vector embeddings and reranking, which can be useful for applications that require offline processing or have strict latency requirements.

#FastEmbed #VectorEmbeddings #Rust #ONNX #LocalProcessing

item.title: Rust SDK Adds Stable 2026-07-28 MCP Version with New Features
item.description:
Rust SDK Adds Stable 2026-07-28 MCP Version with New Features

This release brings the stable MCP 2026‑07‑28 specification to the Rust SDK, while remaining fully compatible with the 2025‑11‑25 release and earlier versions.

🔍 Overview

  • The SDK implements the stable MCP 2026-07-28 specification.
  • It remains fully compatible with the 2025-11-25 release and previous versions.

🧩 Features

  • Server discovery & negotiation
  • Transport‑neutral subscriptions
  • Long‑running tasks
  • Response caching
  • Multi‑round‑trip requests
  • Standard HTTP routing headers

⚙️ SDK Structure

  • Repository crates:
    • rmcp: core crate providing the RMCP protocol implementation
    • rmcp‑macros: procedural macro crate for generating RMCP tool implementations
  • Basic dependencies:
    • tokio
    • serde
  • JSON Schema generation (version 2020‑12):
    • schemars

📦 Installation & Setup

  • Add the latest published version: 
    1

    cargo add rmcp --features server
  • Or use the dev channel: 
    1

    cargo add rmcp --features server --git https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/rust-sdk --branch main

🚀 Server and Client Lifecycle

  • serve() uses the legacy MCP lifecycle:
    • The client sends initialize.
    • The server returns negotiated server information.
    • The client sends notifications/initialized.
  • Use ClientServiceExt::serve_with_lifecycle to select another lifecycle explicitly.
  • ClientLifecycleMode::Initialize is equivalent to the existing serve() behavior.
  • Discover startup does not send notifications/initialized; discovery completes startup.
  • Each subsequent request carries its protocol version, client information, and capabilities in _meta.
  • For a server, serve() waits for peer input that establishes the protocol lifecycle, such as initialize from a legacy client.
  • A stdio MCP server is normally launched by an MCP client as a child process.
  • Running the executable alone in a terminal can leave this await pending because no client has sent protocol messages yet.
  • After serve() returns, the service handles messages in the background.
  • You can run other asynchronous work, then use waiting() to wait for shutdown.
  • To cancel during startup, use serve_with_ct().

🛠️ Building a Service

  • Use ServerHandler or ClientHandler to build a service.
  • Await protocol startup, then receive a handle to the running service.

#Rust #MCP #SDK #Async #JSON

Source: modelcontextprotocol/rust-sdk

item.title: Rust-Powered Multi-Protocol Download Manager Features Dynamic Acceleration and AI Agent Integration
item.description:
Rust-Powered Multi-Protocol Download Manager Features Dynamic Acceleration and AI Agent Integration

A new open-source download manager powered by Rust and the Tokio engine has been released as a free alternative to IDM. The tool features dynamic download acceleration with adaptive segmentation and is designed to be AI-agent ready through a built-in Model Context Protocol (MCP) server.

🔍 Overview

The manager is a local-first, multi-protocol solution that requires no account for local downloads and contains zero advertisements. It uses a shared Rust + Tokio engine that remains independent of the UI and Foreign Function Interface (FFI), allowing it to power various client types from a single core.

  • Multi-protocol support: Handles HTTP/HTTPS, FTP, BitTorrent (including magnet links), eD2K, and streaming via HLS and DASH.
  • Cross-platform clients: Native GPUI desktop apps, Kotlin Android and SwiftUI iOS apps, a React Web UI, and a standalone CLI.
  • Browser integration: Includes a 3-layer interception engine for Chrome, Edge, and Firefox, supplemented by a userscript.

🧩 How it works

The engine implements dynamic download acceleration by splitting segments at runtime. If a segment is performing poorly, idle workers utilize a “slow-segment rescue” feature to take over the task. For persistence, the manager uses SQLite with Write-Ahead Logging (WAL) by default to store resumable states, while server deployments have the option to use PostgreSQL.

Protocol Capabilities
BitTorrent Supports DHT, UPnP, and magnet links
eD2K / eMule Server and Kad DHT source finding with MD4 verification
HLS / DASH Streaming media sniffing and AES-decryption support
Automation RSS subscriptions, scheduled queues, and JavaScript plugins

⚙️ Key details

The software includes professional-grade management tools such as named queues, global token-bucket rate limiting, and connection diagnostics. For developers and power users, it provides several integration paths:

  • AI Readiness: A built-in MCP server with 12 tools allows Claude, Cursor, and other AI clients to manage downloads.
  • Remote Management: Optional FluxCloud device collaboration for settings sync, remote task management, and LAN device pairing.
  • API Support: Offers REST/OpenAPI and aria2-compatible JSON-RPC interfaces.
  • Privacy: Anonymous installation and daily-active statistics can be disabled via settings and do not collect task-specific information.

🚀 Availability

The manager is available across multiple platforms including Windows, macOS, Linux, NAS, and Android. The desktop version includes a system tray service to keep downloads active after the main UI is closed. Users can choose between native GPUI interfaces or a React-based web management console, both supporting light, dark, and custom themes.

#Rust #OpenSource #AIagents #MCP #DownloadManager

Source: zerx-lab/FluxDown

item.title: Nucleoid adds terminal workspace, bare-word syntax, and comment updates
item.description:
Nucleoid adds terminal workspace, bare-word syntax, and comment updates

Nucleoid has updated its developer experience and language syntax with a new full-screen terminal workspace, support for bare-word assignments, and changes to how comments and conditional logic are handled.

🔍 Overview

Nucleoid is a next-generation logic programming language built on structured objects and their relationships, extending the traditional Knowledge Graph. It uses a minimum-token syntax for logic representation and a declarative execution model, eliminating the need for LLMs to manually manage control flow, state propagation, and other imperative constructs.

🧩 How it works

The new interactive interface offers a top-level tab layout, with two tabs reserved for future views. A multiline editor sits at the bottom, featuring autocomplete for keywords, built-ins, and model properties, plus in-session input and result history. Results can be inspected in Text, JSON, or Table formats without re-running the program; arrays of objects render as table rows, while other JSON values display in property/value or index/value views.

Key input behaviors include:

  • Enter inserts a newline.
  • F5 runs the entire editor content.
  • Ctrl-J inserts an automatically indented newline.
  • Tab accepts autocomplete or indents.
  • Ctrl-Space opens suggestions.
  • Ctrl-P / Ctrl-N recalls input while preserving an unfinished draft.
  • F1-F3 switch tabs, F6 changes the result view, and Ctrl-Up / Ctrl-Down select earlier results.
  • Mouse clicks select tabs, views, and results; click/drag edits the cursor/selection, and the wheel scrolls individual panes.
  • Ctrl-C cancels input, Ctrl-Q exits, and .help lists all controls.

⚙️ Key details

  • Assignment Syntax: Assignments can be written as target is value. Quotes are optional around a single word. For example, a is 5 and o.x is "good" are valid. If the value is a bare word that does not match a defined variable, class, function, or built-in, it stores its own text.
  • Conditional Branches: In conditionals like a is A if c else B, a bare word in a branch is read as a variable, class, function, or built-in if it exists; otherwise, it reads as its own text. Parenthesized operands are not treated as words, so a is (A if c else B) requires A and B to be defined.
  • List and Dictionary Items: Inside is values, list items, dictionary values, or named arguments can also be bare words.
  • Comments: Hash (#), double-slash (//), and non-nesting block comments (/* ... */) all work in files and interactive interfaces. Comments take delimiter priority outside literals, meaning // is a comment, not an empty regex (use /(?:)/ for an empty-matching regex). Comments retain newlines and source positions and cannot join tokens or supply indentation. Unclosed block comments report SyntaxError: Unterminated block comment at its opening slash.
  • Plain Mode: Running nucleoid --plain provides a line-oriented interface. Piped stdin or redirected stdout automatically selects this mode. Body lines are prefilled with indentation after the .. prompt, and blank lines submit the block.

🚀 Availability

Install the CLI from crates.io using the command: cargo install nucleoid. The standard nucleoid command opens the full-screen terminal workspace from any directory. File execution and the --json and --graph flags retain their existing behavior. References NUC 76, NUC 93, and NUC 94 document the removal of the --c-style-comments, --is-assignment, and --conditional-words flags, respectively.

#Nucleoid #LogicProgramming #CLI #KnowledgeGraph #Rust

Source: NucleoidAI/Nucleoid

item.title: Claude Opus 5.5 Optimizes SQLite C Extension Performance Beyond Rust Implementation
item.description:
Claude Opus 5.5 Optimizes SQLite C Extension Performance Beyond Rust Implementation

On November 8th, 2026, an investigation using the Claude Opus 5.5 model demonstrated the creation and optimization of a custom SQLite extension. The project focused on developing a parse_number() function to convert strings—such as currency and percentages—into numeric values that can be summed and sorted.

🔍 Overview

The parse_number(value) function was designed with specific parsing capabilities:

  • Strips symbols including ‘,’, ‘$’, ‘£’, and ‘%’.
  • Handles leading ‘-’ characters.
  • Returns ‘NULL’ for any values it cannot successfully parse.

⚙️ Key details

The development process compared building the extension in C versus Rust, revealing significant differences in file size and execution speed:

  • File Size: The C extension resulted in a 14 KB file, while Rust implementations were significantly larger at 321 KB (using Rusqlite) and 298 KB (using sqlite-loadable-rs).
  • Performance Optimization: Although the Rust version was initially faster due to its strtod equivalent being twice as fast as C’s, a custom C function written by the AI achieved superior speeds.

📊 Performance results

The following table displays the net cost per row measured over 2 million rows. Lower values indicate better performance.

Data Type Original C New C Rusqlite (Rust) sqlite-loadable (Rust)
Mixed data 67 ns 19 ns 46 ns 41 ns
Integers only 25 ns 16 ns 36 ns 32 ns
Decimals only 106 ns 18 ns 55 ns 47 ns

🚀 Availability

The final prototype was formatted as a research report for the simonw/research GitHub repository. The model provided the investigation as a downloadable zip file containing the necessary folder structure for the repository.

#SQLite #ClaudeAI #Programming #Rust #C

Source: Research: parse_number() as a SQLite extension: C vs Rust

item.title: Proof‑Driven Development introduced with PDD Kit and Verus for Rust
item.description:
Proof‑Driven Development introduced with PDD Kit and Verus for Rust

Proof‑Driven Development (PDD) arrives as a new software‑development paradigm supported by PDD Kit. The toolkit helps teams turn their intent into formal specifications, automatically proves the generated code for every input, and falls back to tests when a proof cannot reach.

🔍 Overview

  • Coding agents can now generate whole features that span tens of thousands or hundreds of thousands of lines of code.
  • Traditional line‑by‑line review does not scale to this output, and tests often only check what the agent built, not what was originally requested.
  • A plan is meant to be the contract between a developer and an agent, but the agent is not forced to obey it, leading to hidden gaps that surface only as bug reports or edge‑case failures.

🧩 How it works

  1. Intent → Formal Spec – PDD Kit works with you to express the parts of your intent that can be formalized as a specification in Verus.
  2. Proof Generation – The kit automatically generates a mathematical proof that the agent’s code satisfies the formal spec for every possible input.
  3. Fallback to Tests – Anything the proof cannot reach (e.g., third‑party cryptography libraries, UI code) is turned into informal specifications and covered by high‑quality unit, end‑to‑end, terminal‑automation, and browser‑automation tests.
  4. TCB Sign‑off – The boundary between proved code and tested code is the Trusted Computing Base (TCB). PDD Kit makes this line explicit and asks the developer to sign off on each piece.
  5. Collaboration Environment – The workflow runs inside GitHub Next’s Chopin, a real‑time, multiplayer planning environment where teams and agents can co‑author a shared document.

⚙️ Key details

  • PDD Kit – the toolkit that drives the Proof‑Driven Development process.
  • Verus – the verifier used today; a proof language for Rust co‑developed by Microsoft Research, Carnegie Mellon University, VMware Research, ETH Zurich, MPI‑SWS, UNSW Sydney, the University of Texas at Austin, the University of Michigan, the University of British Columbia, the University of Wisconsin–Madison, and the Weizmann Institute of Science.
  • Chopin – the planning interface that lets a team and agents iterate on the plan and proposed tests before handing off implementation.
  • Formal verification – a mathematical proof that code satisfies its specification for every input, providing stronger assurance than testing alone.
  • Evidence vs. Proof – a passing test is labeled as evidence; only a verifier‑checked proof guarantees correctness for all inputs.
  • Real‑world case – inside Chopin, PDD Kit was used to formally verify the login logic of Pet Store, a Rust storefront. Verus hardened the code, uncovered existing bugs, and proved the absence of login bugs with respect to the specification.

💡 Why it matters

  • Proofs cover the entire input space, catching bugs that a test suite—no matter how large—might miss.
  • By making the TCB explicit, teams understand exactly which pieces rely on trust and can review them separately.
  • The approach scales to agent‑generated code where traditional code review is infeasible.
  • It bridges the gap between the plan (the contract) and the shipped code, reducing the hidden mismatch that typically appears only after deployment.

📊 Components at a glance

Component Role
PDD Kit Turns intent into formal specs, generates proofs and tests
Verus Verifier that checks Rust code against formal specs
Chopin (GitHub Next) Real‑time, multiplayer planning environment for teams and agents

#ProofDrivenDevelopment #FormalVerification #AIcodingAgents #Rust

Source: Formally verifying agent-written full-stack web apps with PDD Kit - Microsoft Research

item.title: Rust‑Based docling.rs Speeds Up Document Conversion for LLM Pipelines
item.description:
Rust‑Based docling.rs Speeds Up Document Conversion for LLM Pipelines

The docling.rs project released a Rust port of IBM’s docling that delivers faster, lower‑memory document conversion for LLM and RAG pipelines.

🔧 Overview

  • Converts PDF, Office, HTML, scanned documents, and audio into Markdown, docling JSON, and other formats that LLMs or RAG pipelines can consume.
  • Produces output that is byte‑for‑byte identical to the original IBM docling implementation.
  • Operates as a single static binary – no Python runtime and no PyTorch dependency.

⚙️ How it works

  • Layout analysis, table recognition, and OCR are performed by built‑in ONNX models (layout, OCR, TableFormer, Whisper). These models are bundled (under 1 GB) and can be downloaded once via the provided scripts.
  • Office, HTML, Markdown, and e‑mail formats require no ML models.
  • PDF, images, and audio trigger the ONNX models for full‑fidelity extraction.

🚀 Performance

Format Speedup vs. Python docling RAM usage
PDF 4.3× faster under half
Office & HTML 20–60× faster —
  • Table extraction retains structure with cell recall 0.94, compared to MarkItDown’s 0.31 (see numbers).

🔗 Compatibility with existing stacks

  • MarkItDown: pip install docling-rs and replace the import with from docling_rs.markitdown import MarkItDown. All original formats, layout analysis, tables, and OCR remain functional.
  • Marker: Swap imports to from docling_rs.marker.converters.pdf import PdfConverter and keep the original API (create_model_dict, text_from_rendered, JSON block tree, etc.).
  • MinerU: Replace imports to from docling_rs.mineru.parser import parse and retain MinerU 4’s SDK (ParseResult, markdown(), JSON, Content Lists, save()).
  • Each compatibility guide includes side‑by‑side measurements (MarkItDown, Marker, MinerU).

🌐 Availability

  • Install with pip: pip install docling-rs.
  • Install with npm or from source checkout.
  • Download models once with: 
    1
2

    import docling_rs
docling_rs.download_models()
    or via download_dependencies.sh for non‑Python workflows.
  • Windows support documented in docs/WINDOWS.md.
  • Try the converter directly in the browser (WebAssembly, OCR included) at https://docling-project.github.io/docling.rs/ – processing stays on your device.

📚 Documentation

  • Detailed performance and profiling notes: ./docs/PDF_CONFORMANCE.md#performance--review--profiling-notes.
  • Model download instructions: see the Getting the ML models section referenced in the docs.
  • API migration guides for MarkItDown, Marker, and MinerU are linked in each bullet above.

#docling #Rust #documentconversion #LLM #RAG

Source: docling-project/docling.rs

item.title: Claw Code: Rust‑Based Agent‑Managed Museum Exhibit Using Gajae‑Code and LazyCodex
item.description:
Claw Code: Rust‑Based Agent‑Managed Museum Exhibit Using Gajae‑Code and LazyCodex

An agent-managed museum exhibit called Claw Code has been released. It is a public Rust implementation of the claw CLI agent harness, built with the Gajae-Code and LazyCodex toolchains and designed to run without any human intervention.

🔍 Overview

  • The repository is described as a museum exhibit rather than a commercial product.
  • It is “closer to a museum exhibit than a product pitch,” kept alive by “crab‑run” artifact processes and automatically maintained by agents.
  • The project philosophy explicitly states it is not meant to be hand‑operated like a normal product repo.

🛠️ How It Works

  • The exhibit is agent‑managed: harnesses plan, execute, verify, label, and preserve the artifact while “crabs keep the tank running.”
  • The canonical source lives in the rust/ directory, with the current source of truth being ultraworkers/claw-code.
  • claw is the CLI agent harness; Claw Code provides its public Rust implementation.

📦 Getting Started

  • Start with LazyCodex or Gajae‑Code if you want to run work.
  • For build, authentication, CLI usage, session handling, and parity‑harness workflows, consult USAGE.md.
  • After building, run claw doctor as the first health check.

item.title: Introduction of tokenizers v1 with SIMD and Parallelism Improvements
item.description:
Introduction of tokenizers v1 with SIMD and Parallelism Improvements

A new version of the tokenizers library, v1, has been released. The goal of this version was to improve performance while preserving the API, vocabulary, merge ranks, and output of v0.23, ensuring v1 produces the same token IDs as the previous version.

🧩 How it works

Tokenizers run conversions in four stages:

Stage Description
Normalization Applies operations such as Unicode normalization or lowercasing to raw text.
Pre-tokenization Splits text into smaller pieces called pre-tokens.
Model Maps each pre-token to IDs in its vocabulary.
Post-processing Adds special tokens expected by the model.

⚙️ Key details

BPE and Model Support

  • The library supports three model types: Byte Pair Encoding (BPE), WordPiece, and Unigram.
  • Eight of the ten measured model families use BPE.
  • BPE models use regular expressions to split input text into pre-tokens; merges occur inside a pre-token and never across boundaries.

Performance Optimizations

  • SIMD Instructions: For a handful of common grammars, a hand-written function uses SIMD instructions to find splits via boolean operations over bitstreams instead of a regex engine. This process, using bitcannon, views input bytes as parallel streams and decides 64 bytes per register operation.
  • Memory Management: The merge working set uses a caller-owned scratch buffer to avoid touching the allocator. Merged pieces form an intrusive doubly-linked list inside one preallocated buffer, allowing merges to update two indices rather than moving data.
  • Caching: A thread-local memo maps pre-token bytes to finished IDs, allowing repeated words to be merged once.
  • Concurrency: Each thread draws its scratch buffer and word cache from its own sub-pool, allowing one shared tokenizer to encode from many threads at once without queuing on a single lock.

Architecture Changes

  • The library remains general across tokenizer families and loads everything v0.23 loaded.
  • The project structure moved from one crate to a workspace:
    • tk-encode: The required runtime.
    • tk-serialize, tk-convert, and tk-train: Linked only when an application needs them.

#tokenizers #BPE #SIMD #NLP #Rust

item.title: Targeted Attacks Against Rust Developers and Crate Owners
item.description:
Targeted Attacks Against Rust Developers and Crate Owners

Adam Harvey and the crates security team have issued a warning regarding an ongoing campaign targeting rust-lang members and owners of popular crates to compromise devices and accounts for the purpose of publishing malware.

🧩 How it works

Attackers use video calls framed as positive opportunities—such as projects, jobs, or contract opportunities—as a vector to:

  • Get the target to install software on their computer (e.g., a purportedly missing audio codec).
  • Get the target to execute a command (e.g., via a command placed on the clipboard).

⚙️ Key details

  • Impact: Last month, this method was used in a successful supply chain attack against the array ref crate and others.
  • Risk Factor: Every piece of software depending on open source has a network of human beings who are potential attack vectors, specifically anyone with publishing rights to packages in the dependency network.
  • Defense: A recommended defense is the use of dependency cooldowns, which involves waiting a few days before upgrading to new package releases to allow others to spot supply chain attacks.

#Rust #Cybersecurity #SupplyChainAttack #OpenSource

item.title: AI Agent Skill Translates CUDA Tile Kernels to cuTile Rust
item.description:
AI Agent Skill Translates CUDA Tile Kernels to cuTile Rust

A new AI agent skill has been developed to translate GPU kernels from cuTile Python and Triton-TileIR into cuTile Rust, a tile-based system designed for safe and idiomatic GPU kernel authoring in the Rust programming language.

🔍 Overview

cuTile Rust extends the Rust ownership model to tile-based GPU kernels by splitting mutable outputs into disjoint pieces and preserving the host-side ownership contract across kernel launches. It serves as one of three front ends—alongside cuTile Python and Triton-TileIR—that feed into the same CUDA Tile IR (the cuda_tile dialect) and the tileiras compiler, which emits the GPU binary.

🧩 How it works

The translation process uses a bounded multi-agent pipeline that covers the following stages:

  • Analysis
  • Device kernel creation
  • Host and FFI code generation
  • Benchmarking

Each stage concludes with a machine-checkable verdict. Because all three front ends share the same IR, translation is verified by “diffing” the Tile IR of the reference kernel and the translated kernel to ensure they reproduce the same reductions, tile shapes, and memory-op families before tests are executed.

⚙️ Key details

There are significant differences between the JIT compilation of cuTile Python and the ahead-of-time compilation of Rust source:

  • Specialization: cuTile Python specializes kernels implicitly at call time. In contrast, cuTile Rust requires every specialization to be declared in the kernel’s signature; nothing is specialized unless declared.
  • Structural Changes: A single Python kernel may become multiple Rust entries. For example, layer_norm splits into 2-Dnchw and 1-Dw1 entries because the branch changes tile rank.
  • Compilation: Rust source is compiled ahead of time, with tile shapes and element types checked by rustc. The crate embeds the kernel AST, and the runtime specializes it with concrete const-generic values to compile a cached cubin at first launch.
  • ABI Support: Supporting a dtype is an explicit ABI extension. Supported types include sf32, f16, bf16, i32, i64, f8e5m2, and f8e4m3fn.

🚀 Availability

The translation skill is shipped in the TileGym repo. In TileGym, cuTile Rust functions as a backend that can be activated using tilegym.set_backend("cutile-rs") to route the operator API to Rust kernels.

💡 Why it matters

Using this AI agent skill, all 24 public TileGym operators—comprising roughly 40 GPU kernels—were ported to cuTile Rust. These kernels range from element-wise operations to mixture-of-experts (MoE) models, Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA), and flash-attention decode. On average, the ported kernels reached 99.5% of cuTile Python performance.

#Rust #CUDA #GPU #AIagents #TileGym

Source: Translating CUDA Tile Operations from Python to Rust Using Agentic AI | NVIDIA Technical Blog

item.title: SpaceXAI releases Grok Build: a terminal-based AI coding agent
item.description:
SpaceXAI releases Grok Build: a terminal-based AI coding agent

SpaceXAI has open‑sourced Grok Build, its terminal‑based AI coding agent.

🔍 Overview

  • Grok Build is a terminal‑based AI coding agent developed by SpaceXAI.
  • It runs as a full‑screen text user interface (TUI) that can understand a codebase, edit files, execute shell commands, search the web, and manage long‑running tasks.
  • It can be used interactively, headlessly for scripting/CI, or embedded in editors via the Agent Client Protocol (ACP).

🛠️ How it works

  • The repository contains the Rust source for the grok CLI/TUI and its agent runtime.
  • The source tree is synced periodically from the SpaceXAI monorepo; a SOURCE_REV file records the exact monorepo commit SHA.
  • The workspace Cargo.toml is generated and should be treated as read‑only.
  • Build requirements:
    • Rust toolchain pinned by rust-toolchain.toml; rustup installs automatically on first build.
    • DotSlash is required so hermetic tools under bin/ (e.g., bin/protoc) can be downloaded and run; ensure dotslash is on your PATH before building.
    • protoc proto codegen resolves bin/protoc via DotSlash or falls back to a protoc on PATH / $PROTOC.

⚙️ Key details

  • Supported build hosts: macOS and Linux; Windows builds are best‑effort and not currently tested from this tree.
  • Prebuilt binaries are published for macOS, Linux, and Windows.
  • The binary artifact is named xai-grok-pager; official installs ship it as grok.
  • On first launch the tool opens a browser for authentication (see the authentication guide).
  • Full online documentation: https://docs.x.ai/build/overview
  • User guide location: crates/codegen/xai-grok-pager/docs/user-guide/ (covers getting started, keyboard shortcuts, slash commands, configuration, theming, MCP servers, skills, plugins, hooks, headless mode, sandboxing, and more).

📦 Availability

  • Releases include a changelog with fixes, features, and improvements: https://x.ai/build/changelog
  • Binaries can be downloaded for the three major platforms.

📄 Licensing

  • First‑party code in the repository is licensed under the Apache License, Version 2.0.
  • Third‑party and vendored code retains its original licenses.
  • External contributions are not accepted.
